MorphoHand · SR2 hand, real_v1 · hand–object scale study · 8 October 2026 · built 2026-10-08 23:16

Finger-base spacing against object size on the SR2 hand

Simulated over 17 layouts of the SR2 tripod (thumb–pair span 40–160 mm) and 18 objects (cylinders of 6–80 mm, spheres of 10–160 mm), the best layout for each task grows with the object by a fixed offset rather than in proportion to it. The fixed-contact workspace peaks where the mounts sit the object radius plus 35 (cylinders) or 37 mm (spheres) from its axis or centre, with slope 1.00 and residuals of 0.4 mm rms. That offset is half the 68 mm finger, the rule Borràs and Dollar derived; the ratio of mount distance to radius runs from 1.8 to 12.6. On cylinders, grasp robustness and the held turn of the Wang–Oh–Pollard controller peak on parallel lines inside the workspace ridge: each pad meets the shaft 14, 20 and 23 mm inboard of its mount for the three tasks. On spheres, robustness peaks at the compact edge of each object’s feasible band (8 of 10) and the turn at the wide edge (10 of 10). The contact angle separates the two: straight fingers press face-on and resist pull-out, and bent fingers keep the travel the turn spends. No published study maps finger placement against controlled object size on one physical multi-finger hand. The bench protocol measures both dynamic ridges at 47 cells in 17 bench hours (a core set of eight objects in 7 h of trials), and the paper plan targets RA-L.

Terms and metrics

layoutthe three finger-base (gantry) positions in the palm plane. This study uses symmetric tripods: thumb at , index at , middle at , in mm, with the thumb–pair span and the pair opening. The CAD-nominal hand is .
tripod scale position along the one-parameter layout family (mm), . is real_v1_compact_design(t, t, t); continues to the gantries’ wide limit ( at ).
palm radius radius of the circle through the three mounts, in mm: with . Borràs and Dollar’s “palm radius”; 27.8 mm at , 65.1 at , 102.6 at .
objecta cylinder 100 mm long lying along the pair axis (the screwdriver class) or a sphere, of diameter and radius ; 25 g in simulation.
equator graspthumb pad and both pair pads on the object’s equator (the widest section normal to the pinch axis), the pair straddling the thumb along the cylinder by ± (22.5, 32.5 or 42.5 mm); on a sphere each pad faces its own mount from the centre of the mount circle.
feasiblean equator grasp exists with every joint at least 2.9° (0.05 rad) inside the servos’ calibrated range, the fingertip’s palmar normal within 90° of the object’s inward normal, at least 5 mm between fingers (the clearance gate of real_v1_trajectory_clearance.py), 1 mm between the object and every link and the palm plate.
workspace the fixed-contact precision-manipulation workspace (Borràs and Dollar): each pad centre stays at its point on the object, and counts the object poses (centre on a 3 mm grid, 123 orientations within 45° of the grasp, 15° steps) at which every finger reaches within its joint ranges without collision. Best straddle per cylinder.
rotation rangelargest rotation of the object about the pinch axis (palm ) reachable with the contacts fixed, its centre free, the smaller of the two signs, in degrees (5° steps).
grasp robustness the weakest of six force thresholds, in N: from a held grip, an external force on the object ramps at 4 N/s along ±, ±, ± until the object moves 3 mm or turns 5°; the grip presses each pad with 4 N at rest; 20 N cap. Best of the cell’s grasps; 0 when the grip drops the object.
held turnrotation of the object’s marked axis (along the cylinder; the sphere’s body axis) from horizontal toward vertical at the end of the HOM controller’s hold, in degrees, counted only when at least two fingers each press with at least the object’s weight (0.245 N) and the object is within 20 mm of its start; 0 otherwise. Median of three placements (object offset 2 mm, yaw 2°), best of the cell’s grasps.
HOM controllerthe relative contact-velocity controller of Wang, Oh and Pollard (arXiv 2609.25619) as scripts/hom_turn3.py: contact frames from the TPU block mesh, bounded least squares on the reference relative velocities, pad force regulated to 2 N, 30°/s toward 90°, a governor that stops the reference when a pad’s force falls under 30 % of its target or the object lags by 6°. One parameter set for every cell.
ridge for task and object , the layout of largest score along a family, refined by a parabola through the maximum and its two neighbours; reported as and as the mount distance it implies: for spheres, the half thumb–pair span for cylinders.
reach marginsmallest over the fingers of how far the pad centre can still move away from the MCP axis before the finger is straight, in mm ().
smallest singular value of a finger’s 3×3 pad-position Jacobian, in mm/rad, smallest over the fingers: the slowest direction in which the pad can move.
joint marginsmallest distance of any joint from its servo limit at the grasp, in degrees.
contact anglelargest over the fingers of the angle between the fingertip’s palmar normal and the object’s inward surface normal at the contact, in degrees; 0 = the pad face-on.
force transmissionsmallest over the fingers of the normal pad force produced per N m of the most loaded joint, , in N/(N m): the servo torque margin of the posture.

Prior work on hand–object scale

All 11 works the suggestion note cites exist and say what it attributes to them; 3 needed a correction. Elangovan et al. analyse a two-finger planar gripper whose workspace is largest with the finger bases together; Seo and Armstrong’s grip force falls monotonically with handle diameter over the range they tested, with no optimum; the Bullock, Feix and Dollar result comes from their EMBC 2015 paper. Hota and Kumar’s object is a cylinder, and their under-actuated hand prefers wide bases for every object size. Table 1 gives each source, verdict and finding; docs/experiments/20261008-hand_object_scale/literature.json holds the full records.

No paper sweeps the finger-base geometry of one physical multi-finger hand through five or more settings against several controlled object sizes, and none compares simulated and measured landscapes at the same points for more than three designs. The closest work, which a paper on this map must cite:

  • T. Feix, T. L. Kivell, E. Pouydebat, A. M. Dollar, J. R. Soc. Interface 12(106):20150176, 2015. Modelled thumb-index workspace rises and then falls with object radius over 360 specimens of 38 primate species; the closest modelled analogue of the proposed sweep. (full text)
  • Y. Hao et al., Chinese Control Conference 2016, pp. 6109-6114; J. Bionic Eng. 15(2):220-235, 2018. Only dense physical morphology x size grid found on one device: pull-off force of a soft gripper at 5 finger lengths x 8 spheres (20-90 mm), with a best length per sphere. (abstract)
  • W. G. Bircher, A. M. Dollar, N. Rojas, ICRA 2017, pp. 3453-3460. Simulated and measured reorientation range against object size (20-63 mm) for three built two-finger grippers; the best object size falls from about 48 to 25 mm as the palm narrows. (full text)
  • C. L. Yako, S. Yuan, J. K. Salisbury, IROS 2022, pp. 4638-4645. A simulated optimum of palm width that rises with part radius, for a planar two-finger underactuated grasper; no hardware. (full text)
  • C. M. McCann, A. M. Dollar, ASME IDETC 2018, DETC2018-86149. Three-finger hand, 10,000 designs x 4 object radii in simulation; palm radius dominates the workspace, averaged over object size. (full text)
  • R. R. Ma, A. M. Dollar, J. Mech. Robot. 6(1):011002, 2014. Base separation and object length normalised by finger length: the dimensionless groups a scaling law would use. (full text)
  • J. van der Kamp, G. J. Savelsbergh, W. E. Davis, Dev. Psychobiol. 33(4):351-361, 1998. Children switch from one to two hands at a common cube / finger-span ratio, with hysteresis between ascending and descending size orders. (abstract)
  • T. Feix, I. M. Bullock, A. M. Dollar, IEEE Trans. Haptics 7(3):311-323, 2014. In about 10,000 everyday grasps, 96 % of grasped widths were 7 cm or less: the size range a sweep should cover. (abstract)
  • C. Tian et al., arXiv:2603.00892, 2026. Reconfigurable Bricard palm: 3 palm states x 15 objects (17-180 mm), 3 trials each; the latest configuration-by-size table on hardware. (full text)
  • K. Fay et al., House of Dextra, ICLR 2026, arXiv:2512.03743. Morphology-conditioned co-design in simulation: in-hand rotation correlates with palm-width scale at r = -0.73; object size randomised, not resolved. (full text)

Layout family and object set

The six gantry coordinates of a symmetric tripod reduce to two separations, because the arm re-centres the palm over the object: the thumb–pair span and the pair opening . The one-parameter family runs from the gantries’ widest tripod (, 160 and 170 mm) through the CAD-nominal hand () to the most compact (, 40 and 50 mm); is real_v1_compact_design(t, t, t). Each of the 105 layouts studied (the family at 17 values of , each separation alone at 17 values, and a 9 × 9 grid) sits inside the measured gantry travel: HandPlan’s mount check reports no violation, and the generator bakes each into a real_v1 scene. Figure 1 draws five of them.

Closed-form inverse kinematics of the yaw–MCP–PIP chain (checked against the compiled MuJoCo scene to 0.000 mm, and its clearances against mj_geomDistance to 0.014 mm on 150 grasps) scans every palm height and straddle for an equator grasp. Over the family, cylinders are graspable from 4 to 80 mm and spheres from 8 to 180 mm, and each layout holds a band of diameters that moves with it: cylinders 4–20 mm on the compact tripod, 4–63 on the nominal one and none on the widest; spheres 8–35, 32–100 and 110–180 mm. The pair opening acts against the cylinder: at widening from 50 to 170 mm cuts the largest graspable cylinder from 80 mm to 32 mm at  mm, and to none at 170 mm, because the 100 mm shaft holds the straddle under 42.5 mm and the pair must yaw inward to reach it.

The object set takes eight cylinders and ten spheres across those ranges, roughly geometric in diameter. Each is built to the 25 g of the simulated screwdriver where the geometry allows, as a printed PLA body with a steel rod or ball at the centre and the 40 mm tag on a 2.5 g printed flag; the starred objects cannot reach 25 g and are listed at their built mass. The simulations below hold every object at 25 g.

Fixed-contact workspace and its scaling law

The workspace has a ridge along the family for every object, and the ridge moves to wider layouts as the object grows (Figure 2). Expressed as the mount distance it implies, the ridge is a straight line of slope one in the object radius:

(1)

The fits are over 8 spheres and over 7 cylinders, residuals 0.4 and 0.4 mm rms (Figure 3). The best layout keeps the mounts a fixed 35–37 mm outside the object’s surface, so the ratio is not constant: and run from 1.8 to 12.6 over the set. The offset is half the finger: the straight mount-to-pad chain is 68.1 mm, half of it 34.1 mm. Borràs and Dollar give the same rule for three two-link fingers, with the finger length, although their base joint turns about the palm normal and the SR2 yaw turns about the palm’s axis. The rotation range about the pinch axis peaks along similar lines ( for spheres, for cylinders) and shrinks with size, from 90° on the 10–16 mm spheres to 35° on the 100 mm sphere, because a fixed finger travel turns a larger object through a smaller angle.

Varying one separation at a time shows which of them the object size acts on. With the pair opening held at 110 mm, the cylinder ridge follows the thumb–pair span alone, at 36.4–36.7 mm for every diameter. With the span held at 100 mm, the cylinder’s best pair opening stays at 56–64 mm for every diameter: the pair straddles the shaft along its length, so the opening follows the 100 mm shaft length. A sphere’s ridge moves along both separations (Table 3). A large cylinder therefore wants the thumb moved away from the pair and the pair kept together, and a large sphere wants the whole tripod expanded.

Grasp robustness and reorientation ridges

Each feasible cell of the family was gripped at up to nine grasps (three palm heights spread over its feasible band at each of three straddles; five heights on a sphere): 724 hold tests with twelve disturbance ramps each and 2172 turns of the HOM controller. Each task keeps its own best grasp per cell. Grasp robustness is set by a pull along gravity in 431 of 692 held grips. The weakest torque is a twist about the palm’s axis (the cylinder’s own axis) in 358 of 414 held cylinder grips and 252 of 278 sphere grips, a median 33 and 75 mN m, or 2.9 and 2.6 N at the object’s radius. The controller held the object in 1082 of 1317 cylinder turns and 834 of 855 sphere turns; 1804 of 2172 turns ended at its governor (a pad losing force or the object lagging) and 339 at a joint limit.

On cylinders the three ridges are parallel lines of slope one in the object radius (Figure 3), separated by how far inboard of its mount each finger meets the shaft:

(2)

(6, 7 and 7 cylinders; residuals 0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 mm rms). The pad centre sits  mm from the shaft axis, so at the robustness ridge each pad meets the shaft 14 mm inboard of its mount, at the turn ridge about 20 mm and at the workspace ridge 23 mm. The robust grip wants the thumb 19 mm closer to the pair than the workspace optimum does, at every diameter. Within a cell the tasks choose different grasps as well: the robust grasp is the highest palm of its straddle in 91 of 150 cells, the furthest turn in 48.

On spheres the two dynamic tasks pull to opposite edges of each object’s feasible band, and the workspace ridge lies between them: robustness peaks at the compact edge for 8 of 10 spheres, the held turn at the wide edge for 10 of 10. Toward the wide edge the pair’s contacts move off the pad face toward the 90° limit of the feasible set, which raises the turn and lowers the robustness (Figures 4 and 5).

One variable separates the two dynamic tasks: the contact angle, which grows as the finger bends away from a straight approach. Across the layouts of one object, robustness falls with it (Spearman -0.65 cylinders, -0.66 spheres) and the held turn rises with it (+0.44 cylinders, +0.98 spheres). Straight fingers press face-on and resist pull-out; bent fingers keep the travel the turn spends. Of the variables tested, the reach margin has its own ridge nearest the turn ridge on cylinders (12 mm of thumb–pair span). Table 4 gives every variable.

Point contact on the same TPU block (one convex mesh) ranks the layouts nearly as the pads do. Over the 22 feasible cells of the coarse 5 × 5 grid (), the cell scores of the two models correlate at Spearman 0.89 for robustness and 0.90 for the turn, and each object’s best coarse layout is the same for 7 of 9 objects (robustness) and 7 of 9 (turn). Point contact scores robustness at a median 1.01 and the turn at 0.98 of the pads’ values.

Films of the turn on three layouts

Bench protocol

The protocol measures the two dynamic ridges on hardware at the points the simulation names. The bench grid is every second layout of the family (); for each object it takes the feasible bench layouts within one bench step (15 mm of thumb–pair span) of each simulated ridge, so each ridge is bracketed by three measurements: turn trials at the cells around the turn ridge, ballast series at the cells around the robustness ridge, 47 cells over 17 objects (Table 5). A core set of four cylinders and four spheres, each with both simulated ridges short of the gantries’ end of the family and spread evenly in log diameter (cylinders 6, 10, 25, 63 mm, spheres 10, 16, 50, 100 mm), takes 7.1 hours of trials; the other objects fill the rest of the week. docs/experiments/20261008-hand_object_scale/protocol.json lists the cells with the grasp, the predicted scores and the day plan.

  • Configuration per cell. The six gantry targets of the layout, the cell’s palm pose and the grip and turn commands, exported as a deploy plan (<cell>_plan.json with _traj.csv, the format the station replays). The bench runs the HOM controller’s simulated joint commands open loop, because the hand has no fingertip force sensing; the simulation replays the same file open loop, which is the prediction the bench is compared with at each point.
  • Gates before a cell runs. scripts/real_v1_trajectory_clearance.py on the plan’s chord and its CSV path (at least 5 mm between fingers on both) and HandPlan.validate() (every command inside the servo’s calibrated range, every mount inside the measured gantry travel). A cell that fails either is dropped and logged.
  • Turn trials. 8–15 per cell: the count that puts the 95 % interval of the cell mean within 3°, from the larger of the simulated spread over placements and 4.4°, the median spread of held turns per hand in the eight-hand bench record. The object is placed on its post by hand at the marked pose, the hand grips, the post drops 5 mm, the turn runs, the hand holds 2 s.
  • Grasp robustness. The hanging mass at slip: steel washers added in 5 g steps to a hook under the object until it moves 3 mm or drops, two series per cell at the robust grasp. It measures the pull along gravity, the binding direction of in most simulated grips.
  • Sensing. The AprilTag tracker on the workstation (40 mm tag36h11 on the object’s flag, a static reference tag; 0.017° and 0.03 mm rms when still): the signed cosine of the marked axis with vertical ( = tip down, never the folded tilt), held = tag above the post top 2 s after the turn with at least two fingers on the object, slip = tag translation in the palm frame during the hold.
  • Order. Randomised within each bench day (seed 20261008), so object size and layout are not confounded with time or wear. Each day opens with homing, the tracker check and five trials of the reference cell (nominal layout, 25 mm cylinder) and ends with five trials of two earlier cells; the reference and the revisits measure drift between days.

The 17 bench hours fit one week at five hours of trials a day plus setup. Printing needs the 17 objects of the cell list from Table 2’s recipes; each object is weighed and the simulation re-run at its measured mass before its cells are compared.

Paper plan

Question. How does the best finger-base layout of a three-finger hand with fixed phalanges move with object size, does the answer differ between grasping and in-hand reorientation, and does a simulator with a calibrated contact model predict where the best layout lies?

Contributions.

  1. A dense morphology-by-object-size map on one hardware hand: 17 layouts × 18 objects in simulation and 47 cells on the bench, with the same fingers, servos, tips and controller in every cell.
  2. A scaling law for the kinematic optimum: the best mount distance is the object radius plus about half the finger (37 and 35 mm for spheres and cylinders, slope one), so the best layout grows by an offset while runs from 1.8 to 12.6; the cylinder’s optimum moves the thumb and leaves the pair opening at the shaft’s length scale.
  3. Task-dependent optima: grasp robustness and reorientation select different layouts and different grasps for the same object, separated by the contact angle of the grasp posture.
  4. Agreement of the simulated and measured landscapes at the same points, with the 1 mm pad contact model (calibrated against Drake’s hydroelastic contact) as part of the simulator, and point contact as the comparison.

Venue. RA-L fits contributions 1–3 with the bench agreement in 8 pages; it can be presented at IROS 2027 (deadline around 1 March 2027). T-RO takes the full 2-D map over both separations, the contact-model comparison and the open-loop against closed-loop turn, which do not fit in 8 pages. IJRR suits a framing around SR2 as an experimental morphology instrument with this study as its first use. The recommendation is RA-L, submitted by mid-January 2027, with the extended version for T-RO afterwards.

Timeline. Week of 13 October: export the cell plans, run them through both gates, replay them open loop in simulation, print and weigh the objects. 20 October: the bench week. 27 October: re-simulate at measured masses, sim-to-bench analysis, figures 7–8. November: the 2-D map in simulation for the T-RO version and the writing. Mid-December: internal review. Mid-January: RA-L submission.

Next measurements

  • Open-loop replay of the simulated turn. The bench replays joint commands without force feedback. Record q_cmd in turn_rollout, replay it with hold_rollout’s plant on every cell of the protocol, and recompute the turn ridge; if it moves by more than one bench step (0.25 in ), the bench grid is re-centred on the replay’s ridge.
  • Point-contact check. hand_object_scale_sim.py run --cells coarse --model pt on the 5 × 5 grid; the paper’s contact-model claim needs the pad and point ridges compared object by object.
  • Plan export. A scripts/hand_object_scale_export.py that writes each protocol cell as _plan.json and _traj.csv, then real_v1_trajectory_clearance.py --deploy-dir and HandPlan.validate() on all of them; the cells that fail leave the protocol before printing starts.
  • Mass. Six objects cannot be built at 25 g (Table 2). Re-run their cells at the built mass (MASS in hand_object_scale_sim.py); a ridge that moves by more than one family step means the bench set must hold mass constant by another route (a longer rod, a denser core).
  • The 2-D map. The 9 × 9 grid of separations for the dynamic tasks (about 3 CPU-hours at four processes) answers whether thumb opposition and pair opening scale differently for the turn as they do for the workspace.
  • Grasp elevation. Every grasp here sits on the equator; grasps below it trade depth for wedge stability and are untested.
